title: 29. The fate of the master and Margarita is decided
paragraphs: At sunset, high above the city, on the stone terrace of one of the most beautiful buildings in Moscow, a building constructed about a hundred and fifty years ago, there were two figures: Woland and Azazello. They could not be seen from below, from the street, since a balustrade with plaster vases and plaster flowers screened them from unwanted eyes. But they could see the city almost to its very edges.

Woland was sitting on a folding stool, dressed in his black cassock. His long, broad sword had been stuck upright between two cracked flagstones of the terrace, so that it made a sundial. The shadow of the sword was slowly and steadily lengthening, creeping toward the black shoes on Satan’s feet. Resting his sharp chin on his fist, hunched on the stool with one leg tucked under him, Woland gazed fixedly at the immense agglomeration of palaces, gigantic buildings and little hovels doomed to demolition.

Azazello, having parted with his modern outfit, that is, the jacket, the bowler hat and the patent-leather shoes, and dressed, like Woland, in black, stood motionless not far from his master, and, like him, did not take his eyes off the city.
Woland spoke:
“What an interesting city, is it not?”
Azazello stirred and answered respectfully:
“Messire, I like Rome better.”
“Yes, that is a matter of taste,” Woland replied.
After a while his voice was heard again:
“And what is that smoke over there, on the boulevard?”
“That is Griboyedov’s burning,” Azazello replied.
“One must suppose that the inseparable pair, Koroviev and Behemoth, paid a visit there?”
“There is no doubt about it whatever, messire.”

Again silence fell, and the two on the terrace watched as in the windows turned to the west, on the upper floors of the huge buildings, a broken, dazzling sun was kindled. Woland’s eye burned exactly like one of those windows, although Woland had his back to the sunset.

But here something made Woland turn away from the city and direct his attention to the round tower that stood behind him on the roof. Out of its wall stepped a gloomy man, ragged, smeared with clay, in a chiton and homemade sandals, black-bearded.
“Bah!” exclaimed Woland, looking mockingly at the newcomer. “You are the last person one would have expected here! What brings you here, uninvited but foreseen guest?”
“I have come to you, spirit of evil and lord of shadows,” the newcomer answered, glaring at Woland from under his brows in an unfriendly way.
“If you have come to me, then why did you not wish me good health, former tax collector?” Woland said sternly.
“Because I do not wish you good health,” the newcomer answered insolently.

“But you will have to reconcile yourself to it,” Woland objected, and a smile twisted his mouth. “No sooner had you appeared on the roof than you came out with an absurdity at once, and I will tell you what it is—it is in your intonation. You spoke your words as though you did not acknowledge shadows, nor evil either. Would you be so kind as to think over this question: what would your good do if evil did not exist, and what would the earth look like if the shadows disappeared from it? After all, shadows are cast by objects and people. Here is the shadow of my sword. But there are shadows of trees and of living beings. Do you want to strip the whole globe bare, sweeping away all the trees and every living thing, because of your fantasy of enjoying naked light? You are a fool.”
“I will not argue with you, old sophist,” replied Levi Matvei.
“You cannot argue with me, for the reason I have already mentioned: you are a fool,” Woland replied, and asked: “Well, speak briefly, without tiring me—why have you appeared?”
“He has sent me.”
“And what did he order you to convey, slave?”
“I am not a slave,” replied Levi Matvei, growing more and more embittered, “I am his disciple.”
“We speak different languages, you and I, as always,” responded Woland, “but the things we speak about do not change because of that. Well then?..”
“He has read the master’s work,” Levi Matvei began, “and he asks you to take the master with you and reward him with peace. Is that really hard for you to do, spirit of evil?”
“Nothing is hard for me to do,” Woland replied, “and you know that very well.” He was silent for a while and added: “But why don’t you take him to yourselves, into the light?”
“He has not earned the light, he has earned peace,” Levi said in a sorrowful voice.
“Tell him it will be done,” Woland replied, and added, his eye flaring up: “And leave me at once.”
“He asks that you also take the woman who loved him and suffered because of him,” Levi said, addressing Woland imploringly for the first time.
“We would never have thought of that without you. Go.”
Levi Matvei vanished after this, and Woland called Azazello to him and ordered him:
“Fly to them and arrange everything.”
Azazello left the terrace, and Woland remained alone.

But his solitude did not last long. The tap of footsteps and lively voices were heard on the flagstones of the terrace, and Koroviev and Behemoth appeared before Woland. But now the fat fellow did not have the Primus with him; he was loaded with other objects. Thus, under his arm he had a small landscape in a gold frame, over his arm was flung a cook’s smock, half burned, and in his other hand he held a whole salmon, skin, tail and all. Koroviev and Behemoth reeked of burning, Behemoth’s mug was covered in soot, and his cap was half burned.
“Salute, messire!” cried the irrepressible pair, and Behemoth waved the salmon.
“A fine sight you are,” said Woland.
“Messire, imagine,” Behemoth cried excitedly and joyfully, “they took me for a looter!”
“Judging by the objects you have brought,” Woland replied, glancing at the little landscape, “you are a looter.”
“Would you believe it, messire...” Behemoth began in a heartfelt voice.
“No, I would not,” Woland replied briefly.
“Messire, I swear, I made heroic attempts to save everything that could be saved, and this is all I managed to rescue.”
“You had better tell me why Griboyedov’s caught fire,” said Woland.
Both of them, Koroviev and Behemoth, spread their hands and raised their eyes to heaven, and Behemoth exclaimed:
“I cannot fathom it! We were sitting peacefully, perfectly quietly, having a bite...”
“And suddenly—bang, bang!” Koroviev took up. “Shots! Mad with fear, Behemoth and I rushed off down the boulevard, our pursuers after us, we rushed toward Timiryazev!..”
“But a sense of duty,” Behemoth put in, “overcame our shameful fear, and we went back.”
“Ah, you went back?” said Woland. “Well, then, of course, the building burned to the ground.”
“To the ground!” Koroviev confirmed mournfully. “That is, literally, messire, to the ground, as you were pleased to put it so aptly. Nothing but cinders!”

“I rushed,” Behemoth recounted, “into the meeting hall—that’s the one with the columns, messire—hoping to drag out something valuable. Ah, messire, my wife, if only I had one, would have run the risk of being left a widow twenty times over! But luckily, messire, I am not married, and I’ll tell you frankly—I am happy not to be married. Ah, messire, how can one exchange a bachelor’s freedom for a burdensome yoke!”
“Some sort of nonsense has started again,” observed Woland.

“Understood, and I continue,” replied the cat, “yes, sir, here is the little landscape. Nothing else could be carried out of the hall; the flames struck me in the face. I ran to the storeroom and saved the salmon. I ran to the kitchen and saved the smock. I consider, messire, that I did all I could, and I do not understand what accounts for the skeptical expression on your face.”
“And what was Koroviev doing while you were looting?” asked Woland.
“I was helping the firemen, messire,” replied Koroviev, pointing to his torn trousers.
“Ah, if that is so, then of course a new building will have to be built.”
“It will be built, messire,” responded Koroviev, “I venture to assure you of that.”
“Well, then, it only remains to wish that it be better than the old one,” observed Woland.
“So it will be, messire,” said Koroviev.
“You can take my word for it,” added the cat, “I am a regular prophet.”
“In any case, messire, we have arrived,” Koroviev reported, “and await your orders.”

Woland rose from his stool, went over to the balustrade, and for a long time, silent and alone, with his back turned to his retinue, gazed into the distance. Then he stepped away from the edge, sat down again on his stool and said:

“There will be no orders—you have done all you could, and for the present I have no further need of your services. You may rest. A storm will come now, the last storm; it will complete all that needs completing, and we shall set off on our way.”
“Very good, messire,” the two buffoons answered, and disappeared somewhere behind the round central tower that stood in the middle of the terrace.

The storm Woland had spoken of was already gathering on the horizon. A black cloud rose in the west and cut off half the sun. Then it covered it entirely. It grew cooler on the terrace. A little while later it became dark.

This darkness, which came from the west, covered the enormous city. The bridges and palaces vanished. Everything disappeared, as though it had never existed in the world. A single fiery thread ran across the whole sky. Then a thunderclap shook the city. It came again, and the storm began. Woland could no longer be seen in its murk.
